prompt: Suppose $\int_1^5 f(x) \, dx = 8$ and $\int_1^3 f(x) \, dx = 3$. Find $\int_3^5 \left(2f(x) + 1\right) dx$.
hint: The interval from $1$ to $5$ splits into a piece from $1$ to $3$ and a piece from $3$ to $5$. How can the two known integrals give you $\int_3^5 f(x) \, dx$?

hints.text: The interval from $1$ to $5$ splits into a piece from $1$ to $3$ and a piece from $3$ to $5$. How can the two known integrals give you $\int_3^5 f(x) \, dx$?
Subtracting gives $\int_3^5 f = 8 - 3 = 5$. Then split the new integral with linearity: $\int_3^5 (2f + 1) \, dx = 2 \int_3^5 f \, dx + \int_3^5 1 \, dx$.
The value is $2(5) + (5 - 3) = 10 + 2 = 12$, so the integral equals $12$.

explanation: Integrals add over adjacent intervals: $\int_1^5 f = \int_1^3 f + \int_3^5 f$, so $\int_3^5 f = 8 - 3 = 5$.
Linearity lets you split the sum and pull out the constant: $\int_3^5 (2f + 1) \, dx = 2\int_3^5 f \, dx + \int_3^5 1 \, dx = 2(5) + 2$.
The total is $12$. The $\int_3^5 1 \, dx = 2$ term is the width of the interval, which is easy to forget.

alternativeExplanations.title: Think in areas
steps: Adding $1$ lifts the graph by $1$ over an interval of width $2$, adding a $2 \times 1$ rectangle of area $2$.
